description_ru: Путевой очерк о Лиссабоне: трамваи, смотровые площадки, пирожные и фаду в городе, построенном на холмах.
text:
Lisbon is a city that makes your legs ache and your heart happy. It is built on seven hills, and almost every street seems to go either steeply up or sharply down, so the first piece of advice any local will give you is to wear comfortable shoes. The second piece of advice is to forget the idea of a quick visit. A city like this cannot be rushed, and the people who try to see it in a single day usually go home exhausted and slightly disappointed.

The best place to begin is Alfama, the oldest district, which survived the great earthquake of 1755 because it was built on firm rock. The earthquake, followed by a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of the lower town, and the rebuilding was carried out according to a new grid plan, which is why the streets of the Baixa district are straight and the streets of Alfama are twisted like a bowl of spaghetti. Getting lost there is not a risk but a pleasure, and nobody will blame you for it.

Everyone talks about Tram 28, and it deserves its reputation, but it also deserves a warning. The little yellow carriages, which were built in the 1930s, rattle through the narrowest streets of the old town, and in summer the queue at the first stop can be longer than the journey itself. I was told by my hotel receptionist to board near the end of the line, where it is quieter, and the advice turned out to be excellent. We found seats at once, and the driver even waved at a pigeon.

Lisbon has a tradition of viewpoints, called miradouros, and visiting several of them is the best way to understand the shape of the city. From the terrace of Santa Luzia, you look down at the red roofs and the blue strip of the river, while an old man in a cap sells small glasses of ginjinha, a sweet cherry liqueur. If you are travelling with children, you might choose lemonade instead, although the children, I noticed, were more interested in the pigeons.

Another detail that visitors notice quickly is the tiles. Almost every building seems to be covered with azulejos, painted ceramic tiles in blue, yellow and green, which were introduced by the Moors and later adapted by Portuguese artists. Some of them show saints, ships and battles, while others are simple geometric patterns. There is even a museum devoted to them, where one panel, showing the whole city before the earthquake, is more than twenty metres long. It is worth spending an hour there, especially on a rainy day.

The streets are also decorated with another handmade art. The pavements in many parts of the city are made of small pieces of limestone and basalt, laid by hand into patterns of waves and stars. They look beautiful, but when they are wet, they become as slippery as ice, so walk carefully. I saw a man in a business suit slide gracefully for three metres, recover his balance and walk on without a flicker of embarrassment, as if he had planned it.

No visit would be complete without food. The most famous treat is the pastel de nata, a small custard tart with a crisp, flaky crust and a burnt top. A bakery in the western district of Belem has been making them since 1837, according to a recipe that is said to be known by only a few people. The tarts are served warm, with cinnamon and sugar on the side, and a single tart is never enough. For a proper meal, try grilled sardines in June, when they are at their best, or a bowl of caldo verde, a green soup made with kale and potato.

In the evening, the city changes character. Small restaurants in Alfama and the neighbouring district of Mouraria offer fado, a type of music that is full of longing and nostalgia, usually sung by a single voice with Portuguese guitar. The Portuguese word saudade, which is often translated as a feeling of missing something that is gone, is said to describe the mood. When the singer begins, the waiters stop moving, the glasses stop clinking and everyone is expected to be silent. Even if you do not understand a single word, it is difficult to remain unmoved.

If you have a few days to spare, take a short train ride to Sintra, a hillside town about forty minutes away. Its palaces, which were built for kings and aristocrats, look like illustrations from a fairy tale, and the forest around them is so damp and green that it feels like another country. Go early, because the crowds arrive by ten, and bring a jacket, since the weather in the hills can be several degrees cooler than in the city.

On my last evening, I climbed to a small terrace near my hotel and watched the sun go down behind the river. A group of students were playing guitar, and a woman was selling grilled chestnuts from a little cart. Nobody was in a hurry. I realised that I had been walking uphill for five days and had hardly noticed it, because every hill had a reward at the top. That, I think, is the real secret of Lisbon.

questions.question: Why did Alfama survive the 1755 earthquake?
questions.answer: It was built on firm rock.

questions.question: What advice did the receptionist give about Tram 28?
questions.answer: To board near the end of the line where it is quieter.

questions.question: What is a pastel de nata?
What is fado?
questions.answer: A type of music full of longing, sung with Portuguese guitar.
